original_value: The optimal diversity management problem (ODMP) arises in many application fields when a company, producing a good and/or a service customizable with options, has to satisfy many different client demands with various subset of options, but only a limited number of option combinations can be produced. ODMP can be represented by a disconnected network and formulated as a large‐scale ‐median problem (PMP). In this article we improve a known decomposition approach where smaller PMPs, related to the network components, can be solved instead of the initial large problem. The proposed method is structured in three stages and it combines Lagrangian relaxation‐based techniques, variable fixing and reduction tests, and a dynamic programming algorithm. It drastically reduces the number and the dimensions of the ‐median subproblems to be solved to optimality by a MIP solver and to be combined to determine the optimal solution of the original PMP by a multiple choice knapsack problem. A sequential and a parallel implementation of the method are provided and tested. Obtained results on known and new test instances show that our approach considerably outperforms state‐of‐the‐art algorithms for large‐scale ODMPs.

result.paraphrase: The optimal diversity management problem (ODMP) appears in many application areas when a company offering a customizable good and/or service must meet numerous client requests involving different subsets of options, while only a limited set of option combinations can be produced. ODMP can be modeled as a disconnected network and posed as a large-scale -median problem (PMP). In this article, we enhance a well-known decomposition strategy in which smaller PMPs associated with the network components are solved instead of the original large problem. The proposed approach has three stages and integrates Lagrangian relaxation techniques, variable fixing and reduction tests, and a dynamic programming algorithm. It greatly cuts down both the number and size of the -median subproblems that must be solved to optimality by a MIP solver and then combined, via a multiple choice knapsack problem, to obtain the optimal solution of the original PMP. Sequential and parallel implementations of the method are presented and evaluated. Results on known and newly generated test instances show that our approach substantially outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms for large-scale ODMPs.
